shortSummary: Viljami Kuosmanen describes epilot's experiment giving non-engineers coding agents through Slack. Shared documentation, preview links and engineer review enabled contributions across product, design, support and QA, while a deployment near miss exposed permission gaps and review became a bottleneck.
longSummary: Viljami Kuosmanen describes an epilot workflow in which people tag a coding agent in a Slack discussion, receive a pull request and inspect a preview before an engineer reviews the change. Bringing agents into an existing communication channel lowered setup friction and made examples visible across the company. Agents receive codebase conventions and business context through shared documentation. Product managers, designers, customer-success staff and QA then contributed changes and prototypes, sometimes across repositories. Viljami also describes an attempted production deployment that monitoring caught, followed by tighter merge and CI permissions and separation of production access from developer machines. More generated proposals increased the work of review and testing, and rejected pull requests remained part of the process. He reports substantial contribution counts, while explicitly saying he does not yet have strong data establishing a delivery-speed improvement.

takeaways.point: Put the agent where work and its context already happen; visible Slack threads also let colleagues learn from one another.
A shared body of codebase and business documentation is a central input to useful agent work.
Preview links let non-engineers inspect and test a change without a local development setup.
Contribution access, merge rights, CI permissions and production access need distinct controls.
More proposals create review and testing work; a high contribution count does not establish productivity, and some PRs should be discarded.
